extracted.intended_audience: literary critics and writers of criticism (especially English/Victorian critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for practising and evaluating literary/intellectual criticism: how a critic should conduct criticism, what aims it should pursue, and what anti-patterns to avoid (political partisanship, polemic, personal attack).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The rule may be summed up in one word, — disinterestedness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism must keep aloof from 'the practical view of things' and resolutely follow its own law: a free play of the mind on all subjects. It should refuse to lend itself to ulterior political or practical considerations even when such considerations are commonly attached to ideas. Disinterestedness implies treating knowledge and thought as valuable in themselves and avoiding instrumentalisation of criticism for party aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep aloof from practical/political applications
rubrics_metrics.description: "By keeping aloof from what is called 'the practical view of things:' by resolutely following the law of its own nature..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not transport ideas abruptly into the world of politics and practice; criticism's business is not to decide or implement practical consequences. Anti-pattern: critics acting as ministers of political or sectarian interests or insisting on practical applications rather than intellectual value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and make known "the best that is known and thought"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Its business is... simply to know the best that is known and thought in the world, and by in its turn making this known, to create a current of true and fresh ideas."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise discovery, understanding, and dissemination of high intellectual and artistic achievement. Evaluation should measure a work by how it approaches the best available thought and how criticism helps create a living intellectual current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from parties, sects, and interests
rubrics_metrics.description: "There should be a criticism... absolutely and entirely independent of them [sects and parties]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid being an organ for a political, religious, or social faction (e.g., the Edinburgh Review as an organ of Whigs). Independent criticism gains authority and is better able to advance genuine ideas. Anti-pattern: criticisms subordinated to party aims, used to prop up practical agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid polemical, controversial, or merely practical criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is because criticism has so little kept in the pure intellectual sphere, has so little detached itself from practice, has been so directly polemical and controversial, that it has so ill accomplished... its best spiritual work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should not primarily be combative or reactionary; polemical energy that serves immediate practical ends usually narrows and vulgarises thought. Instead, criticism should aim for reflective, contemplative treatment even if this is less dramatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inflexible honesty and due ability
rubrics_metrics.description: "Its business is to do this with inflexible honesty, with due ability; but its business is to do no more."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics must be sincere, rigorous, and competent. Integrity of judgment matters more than pleasing factions or producing popular impact. Assessments should be honest and based on genuine expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate free intellectual curiosity (disinterested curiosity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism "obeys an instinct prompting it to try to know the best that is known and thought in the world, irrespectively of practice..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value curiosity in the high sense: a disinterested love of free play of the mind on all subjects. Encourage exposure to foreign thought and varied ideas; small infusions of such thought broaden intellectual life. Anti-pattern: dismissive nationalism or contempt for 'curiosity' as a trivial vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience: accept subtle, indirect, and slow influence
rubrics_metrics.description: "It will be said that it is a very subtle and indirect action which I am thus prescribing for criticism... Slow and obscure it may be, but it is the only proper work of criticism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise criticism's effects are often gradual and indirect. Do not expect immediate practical change; long-term intellectual formation is the critic's legitimate aim. Anti-pattern: expecting instant political consequences or quick popular reforms from criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain collectedness and fine distinctions to avoid misunderstandings
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must "remain collected, and refusing to lend himself to the point of view of the practical man..." and make "fine distinctions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep composure and nuance; present intentions clearly to reassure practical-minded readers and avoid being misconstrued as hostile to practical aims. Preserve subtle distinctions that practical audiences may overlook; criticism's value often lies in such refinements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use criticism to check self-satisfaction and promote perfection by establishing contrasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism's spiritual work is "to keep man from a self-satisfaction which is retarding and vulgarising, to lead him towards perfection, by making his mind dwell upon what is excellent in itself..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should juxtapose claims of national/practical triumph with inconvenient facts (e.g., juxtaposing eulogies of 'unrivalled happiness' with the grim news of social ills) to moderate excessive pride and stimulate moral and aesthetic improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal attack and gratuitous controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Author's practice: "So sincere is my dislike to all personal attack and controversy, that I abstain from reprinting... the essays in which I criticised Dr. Colenso's book... I feel bound... to make here a final declaration of my sincere impenitence for having published them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from ad hominem assaults and vindictive polemics. Even when criticizing serious errors, maintain civility and focus on ideas rather than personal vilification. Anti-pattern: harsh public personal attacks that obscure the intellectual point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge works solely by their practical consequences or popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The practical consequences of a book are to genuine criticism no recommendation of it, if the book is, in the highest sense, blundering."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works on intellectual and aesthetic merits rather than their immediate usefulness to a political cause or their popular appeal. A book's practical helpfulness does not excuse conceptual or methodological confusion.
